coreTruths.title: In the polytrauma patient the face waits: airway, breathing, and circulation come first
coreTruths.broaderContext: Most trauma deaths happen in the first hour. ATLS gives one safe sequence to keep the patient alive before any facial work begins, and dental teams should know it cold.
coreTruths.body:
## ATLS exists because the first hour is where most lives are lost or saved

The trimodal pattern of trauma deaths puts the second peak inside the first hour, and that is the window ATLS targets [1]. The system is one safe way to resuscitate, not the only way, and the principles overlap with basic life support that any GDP should be ready to apply in the surgery [2].

## ABCDE forces the lethal injury to be treated first

The primary survey runs Airway with cervical spine control, Breathing, Circulation with haemorrhage control, Disability, Exposure, in that order, with resuscitation happening alongside [3]. Definitive care, including anything to the face, only follows the primary survey, X-rays, and a stable secondary survey [4].

## Maxillofacial injuries do not jump the queue

Unless the facial injury itself is wrecking the airway, threatening the cervical spine, or exsanguinating, it waits [5]. Intracranial, visceral, and major orthopaedic injuries with neurovascular compromise get sorted first. Isolated facial trauma rarely bleeds enough to cause hypovolaemic shock, so a shocked patient with a facial injury almost certainly has another bleed somewhere [6].

## Maxillofacial trainees and anyone managing trauma should do the course

ATLS is built for front-line physicians, but oral and maxillofacial trainees can sit it, and it is strongly recommended for anyone who may take on a trauma patient [7].

citations.quote: These have a trimodal distribution. The first peak is within seconds to minutes of injury. The second is within the first hour, the ‘golden hour’, and is the area of main concern. The third is days to weeks later but may reflect management within the golden hour.

ATLS is a system providing one safe way of resuscitating a trauma victim. It was first conceived in Nebraska, subsequently developed by the ACS, and has now reached international acceptance. It is not the only approach but it is one which works. The principles of basic life support are included during trauma management and can be applied during emergencies in general dental practice.
This uses the mnemonic ABCDE on the basis of identifying and treating the most lethal injury first.
The core concept is the primary survey with simultaneous resuscitation, followed by a secondary survey leading to definitive care.

Other than those with a direct effect on the airway or cervical spine, or causing exsanguinating haemorrhage, maxillofacial injuries should not be dealt with until the ABCs have been completed and this question should be asked of all referring doctors prior to accepting responsibility for a patient. Intracranial, visceral, and major orthopaedic injuries with neurovascular compromise should be identified and managed first.

Remember that isolated facial injuries rarely cause sufficient bleeding to induce hypovolaemic shock. Bleeding can cause pressure to the optic nerve and can cause blindness. Visual acuity must be checked.

While ATLS is designed primarily for front-line physicians, dental graduates training in oral and maxillofacial surgery can complete the course, and it’s strongly recommended to anyone who may undertake care of the trauma patient.

coreTruths.title: Head injury and the eye dictate urgency, not the broken bones
coreTruths.broaderContext: Patients die from intracranial injury and lose vision from retrobulbar bleeds. Both can sit beside an obvious facial fracture and steal attention from the real threat.
coreTruths.body:
## Conscious level is the single most important sign

A change in level of consciousness is the earliest and most valuable sign of head injury [1]. The Glasgow Coma Scale plus pupillary response, respiration, pulse, BP, and limb movement is what is tracked, and a 2-point GCS drop is significant — beware staff handovers masking it [2]. Severe injury sits at GCS under 8, moderate 9 to 12, minor 13 to 15, with under 6 in the absence of drugs carrying a dismal prognosis [3].

## Late vital signs flip the textbook

In raised intracranial pressure the pulse drops and the BP rises, and respiration slows [4]. By the time those show up the window is closing. The work in the meantime is preventing secondary brain injury: oxygenate, control PCO2 with moderate hyperventilation, control bleeding, give tranexamic acid, get neurosurgery on the phone, and keep steroids out of it [5].

## Visual acuity must be documented in every facial trauma

Any facial injury can hide a retrobulbar haemorrhage, an arterial bleed behind the globe, which is a surgical emergency. It presents as a painful, proptosed eye with falling vision [6]. The eye is decompressed by lateral canthotomy with mannitol, acetazolamide, and steroids as a holding measure while theatre is arranged [6]. So vision gets checked and recorded, with a Snellen chart where possible, and any drop triggers ophthalmology [7].

## CT is the definitive scan but only after the patient is stable

CT defines what is going on inside the skull and is the imaging of choice for the cervical spine and Le Fort fractures [8]. The line is firm: never transfer a patient for scanning before correcting hypoxia and hypovolaemia [8].

citations.quote: Change in the level of consciousness is the earliest and most valuable sign of head injury.
A change in GCS score of 2 or more is significant. Beware changes in monitoring staff!
Severe: <8. Moderate: 9–12. Minor: 13–15.
d pulse and ↑ BP is a late sign of ↑ intracranial pressure.

You are preventing 2° brain injury: Oxygenate. Moderate hyperventilation to control partial pressure of carbon dioxide (PCO2). Control haemorrhage and optimize fluid balance, use tranexamic acid. Contact neurosurgery and ask advice. Only use mannitol under expert advice.

This is an arterial bleed behind the globe following trauma. It presents as a painful, proptosed eye with decreasing visual acuity, and is a surgical emergency. The clot must be decompressed and evacuated. Medical management with mannitol 20% 2g/kg, acetazolamide 500mg and prednisolone at least 1mg/kg all IV may help while theatre is being arranged. Evacuation is by lateral canthotomy. Involve ophthalmology.

Orbital compartment syndrome (retrobulbar haemorrhage), …… Retrobulbar haemorrhage, p. 496. Assess and document visual acuity, can they count fingers? Use a Snellen chart to formally document vision. If evidence of lost or decreasing visual acuity, request formal ophthalmological review.
The definitive investigation. However, patients must be stabilized first. Never transfer a patient before correcting hypoxia and hypovolaemia.

coreTruths.title: Facial fracture treatment is reduction, fixation, immobilization — and ORIF changed the game
coreTruths.broaderContext: The mandible and mid-face heal predictably when the fragments are returned to their pre-injury position and held there. Open reduction with plates is what made that reliable.
coreTruths.body:
## The principle is simple: put the bones back, hold them there

All facial fracture treatment boils down to reduction, fixation, and immobilization of the fragments [1]. Historically the mandible and maxilla were locked in occlusion with intermaxillary fixation. Today elastic traction is used to supplement internal fixation rather than replace it [1].

## ORIF revolutionized facial fracture management

Open reduction and internal fixation lets the fracture be exposed through mucosal incisions, reduced under direct vision, and held with bone plates and monocortical screws. IMF can then come off for recovery, replaced by elastics on the ward if needed [2]. Resorbable plates exist but have not yet matched titanium for reliability [2].

## Diagnosis of a mandibular fracture turns on the bite and the lingual sulcus

The pathognomonic combination is the patient unable to bite their teeth or dentures together as they normally do, plus a lingual mucosal haematoma [3]. Step deformities, bony crepitus, IDN paraesthesia, and trismus under 40 mm round out the picture. DPT plus PA mandible are the essential plain films, and condylar fractures need CT before fixation [4].

## Children and condyles are managed differently

Under 12, condylar fractures do best with analgesia, soft diet, and intermaxillary elastic guidance if needed. Over 12, the aim is pain-free pre-injury occlusion within 7 days, and ORIF if that cannot be achieved spontaneously [5]. White eye blowout in children, with intractable vomiting and no subconjunctival haemorrhage, is one of the rare emergencies — operate within 48 hours [6].

## Teeth in the fracture line are not automatically removed

Wisdom teeth and grossly broken or periodontally infected teeth in the fracture line come out. Otherwise, antibiotics, adequate reduction, good follow-up, and endodontics as a secondary procedure usually preserve teeth in the line [1].

citations.quote: Essentially involves reduction, fixation, and immobilization of the # segments. In mandibular and maxillary #, this was traditionally achieved by IMF, i.e. immobilizing the jaws in occlusion. Nowadays, elastic traction is sometimes used to supplement internal fixation. Wisdom teeth and grossly broken down or periodontally infected teeth in the # line should be removed. Otherwise, provision of antibiotics and adequate reduction and immobilization with good follow-up (including endodontics as a 2° procedure) often allows preservation of teeth in the # line.

ORIF of facial bone # has revolutionized Rx. # sites are exposed, usually via mucosal incisions, and reduced under direct vision; the teeth are placed in temporary IMF &/or a wire around the tooth on either side of the # (tension band or bridle wire) and small bone plates fixed by monocortical screws are placed to immobilize the reduction. IMF can then be released for recovery and elastics placed instead on the ward if needed. Resorbable plating systems are now on the market (polylactic and polyglycolic acid) but are yet to match titanium’s reliability.
Ask if the patient can bite their teeth or dentures together in the manner which is normal to them. Inability to do this and a lingual mucosal haematoma is pathognomonic of a mandibular #.

DPT and PA mandible are the essentials in order to diagnose and assess a mandibular fracture. Most patients in trauma centres will have additional assessment with a CT scan. CT scans are required to assess condylar fractures before fixation.

Management depends on age and type of injury. <12yrs: analgesia, soft diet, and intermaxillary elastic guidance (if needed) produces optimal results. >12yrs: pain-free, pre-injury occlusion should be established (by elastic traction if need be), and the patient reassessed at 7 days. If spontaneous pain-free occlusion not possible at this stage: ORIF.

Seen in children, often a trapdoor blowout # with no subconjunctival haemorrhage but severe pain and intractable vomiting. Repair resolves the condition. Rare but one of the few indications for emergency orbital surgery.

coreTruths.title: TMJ surgery is a last resort: most joint problems settle with conservative measures
coreTruths.broaderContext: TMJ disorders are mostly self-limiting or muscular. Surgery has a role for true ankylosis, recurrent dislocation, and end-stage arthritis, but most patients should never see a scalpel.
coreTruths.body:
## Ankylosis splits into true and false, and the distinction changes everything

True ankylosis is restriction of movement caused by the joint itself, usually after intracapsular fracture in childhood or infection. Fibrous union responds to exercises; bony union needs interpositional arthroplasty or condylectomy with reconstruction, with post-operative exercise crucial [1]. False ankylosis, restriction from outside the joint, is rare and treated by addressing the cause [2]. Trismus, often muscular spasm with opening under 40 mm, is much commoner and gets confused with ankylosis, but the joint is fine [2].

## Dislocation is reduced manually, almost always under LA

The vast majority of TMJ dislocations can be reduced under local anaesthesia around the joint, with sedation if needed. Thumbs go over the molars (or in the buccal sulcus once LA is in place to avoid being bitten) with downward and backward pressure [3]. Patients are advised to support the jaw when yawning. Recurrent dislocators can often be taught to self-reduce, which avoids IMF [3]. Sclerosants are out of fashion, and no surgical technique has won the field, although eminectomy is the most common [3].

## Osteoarthrosis of the TMJ runs a different course from other joints

It is degenerative cartilage disease but most patients have symptoms for about a year that fade over the next two, with the condyle remodelling to a flat smooth surface and a long remission following [4]. Treatment is pain relief using standard TMD measures [4]. Intra-articular steroids are reserved for those who fail those, with high condylar shave or condylectomy if pain persists 3 to 4 months later, and total joint replacement as a last resort [4].

## Joint replacement is reserved for end-stage disease in subspecialist hands

Custom condyle and fossa replacements exist, but they are kept for severe symptomatic end-stage joint disease and should be done by those with a sub-specialist interest [5].

citations.quote: True ankylosis is restriction of movement caused by a pathological joint condition, usually due to trauma (intracapsular # in childhood) or infection. Extreme limitation of movement and X-rays will confirm degree of bony union. In fibrous union, exercises are of value. In bony union, interpositional arthroplasty or condylectomy with reconstruction is needed. Post-operative exercise is crucial.

Restriction of movement imposed by extra-articular abnormalities is very rare. Rx depends upon cause. Trismus (interincisal opening ~<40mm, is often due to limitation of movement due to spasm of muscles of mastication), this may be confused with ankylosis but does not affect the joint. It is much more common and complicates many oral surgical procedures; may follow trauma or infection, may be a manifestation of occult malignancy, or a response to treatment, e.g. radiotherapy.

Rx: immediate reduction; the vast majority can be performed with LA around the dislocated joint &/or sedation. Place thumbs over molar teeth and exert downward and backward pressure (if LA is used, less force is needed and thumbs can be placed in buccal sulcus, avoiding the risk of being bitten). Advise jaw support when yawning, etc.; this is usually enough, and avoids IMF. In chronically recurring dislocations, patients can be taught to self-reduce. Exercises are of limited benefit but may avoid surgery. Sclerosant injections are unpleasant and no longer used. Operations are legion; capsular plication, pins to augment articular eminence, Dautrey down-fracture of zygomatic arch, obliteration of upper joint space, eminectomy, high condylectomy. No one operation has gained pre-eminence although eminectomy is probably the most favoured.

A distinct entity of the TMJ, with a different clinical course from that seen in other joints. Appears to be a degenerative condition of articular cartilage. ∆: crepitus, limitation, and pain on movement, tenderness over condyle, often with X-ray evidence of condylar erosions. Most have symptoms for ~1yr which gradually ↓ over the next 2yrs. X-rays show condylar remodelling to a flat smooth surface. Patients then enter a long period of remission. Rx is therefore aimed at pain relief, using standard TMD measures (…… Temporomandibular pain—dysfunction/facial arthromyalgia, p. 484). Those remaining unresponsive may benefit from intra-articular steroids (…… Intra-articular steroids, p. 602), which probably accelerate natural remodelling. A small group will remain with pain 3–4 months after steroids, usually with X-ray abnormalities. They should be considered for high condylar shave or high condylectomy. Rarely, total joint replacement is appropriate.

A handful of specifically designed customized condyle and fossa replacements are available. These should be reserved for severe symptomatic end-stage joint disease in the hands of those with a sub-specialist interest.

coreTruths.title: Orthognathic surgery is functional first; managing motivation and expectations is half the work
coreTruths.broaderContext: Skeletal-deformity surgery is long, complex, and irreversible. The primary indications are functional, but patients want a face change. Aligning those views before starting matters as much as the cuts.
coreTruths.body:
## Functional indications come first, aesthetics second

Orthognathic surgery treats facial skeletal deformity and overlaps with cleft and craniofacial work [1]. The primary indications are functional — speech and eating. Aesthetics are a secondary indication, even though that is often what brings the patient in [1].

## Patient motivation and the limits of surgery have to be on the table early

Patients do not always see function and appearance as separate. Their reasons and motivation must be understood, and the limits of surgery made absolutely clear, before embarking on protracted and complex treatment [2]. The conversation is part of consent, not a courtesy.

## The toolkit splits into mandibular and maxillary procedures

Mandibular procedures act on ramus, body, alveolus, or chin. Sagittal split osteotomy is the workhorse, moving the mandible forward or back, with paraesthesia of the IDN as the main complication [3]. Genioplasty repositions the chin tip and is effective for obstructive sleep apnoea [4]. On the maxilla, Le Fort I down-fracture is the mainstay, freeing the maxilla on a palatal pedicle to move it up, down, or forward; posterior movement is more difficult [5].

## Stability comes from soft tissues, occlusion, and pre-surgical orthodontics

Mini-plates have reduced reliance on bone grafts. Pre-surgical orthodontics drives down relapse, and IMF or elastic traction remains vital long-term [6]. The strongest anti-relapse measures are good dental interdigitation and planning movements that the soft tissue envelope can actually accommodate [6].

citations.quote: This is the surgery of facial skeletal deformity and merges with cleft and craniofacial surgery. 1° indications are functional: speech, eating. 2° indications are aesthetic.

Patients may not see these as quite such separate issues. Their reasons and motivation for seeking surgery must be understood and the limitations of surgery made absolutely clear before embarking on protracted and complex Rx.

Can move mandible backwards or forwards. IO incision similar to intra-oral vertical subsigmoid osteotomy. Bone cuts made from above lingula, across retromolar region, down buccal aspect to lower border. Split sagittally with an osteotome followed by spreaders. Main complication is paraesthesia of IDN.

The tip of the chin can be moved pretty much anywhere; the secret is to keep a sliding contact with bone and a muscle pedicle. Fixation should be kept away from areas of muscle activity as this leads to bone resorption. Effective treatment for obstructive sleep apnoea.

Mainstay procedure. Standard approach is the ‘down-fracture’ with horseshoe buccal incision, bone cuts at Le Fort I level, and segment pedicled on the palate. The freed maxilla can be moved up, down, or forward. Posterior movement more problematic.

i use of mini-plates in the fixation of the osteotomized segments has ↓ the reliance on bone grafts. Pre-surgical orthodontics (…… Pre-surgical orthodontics, p. 168) makes a significant contribution to ↓ rate of relapse. IMF &/or elastic traction remains vital for long-term success. Good dental interdigitation, and planning movements within the capacity of the soft tissues, are probably the best anti-relapse measures.

coreTruths.title: In a salivary gland mass, pain, rapid growth, and facial nerve signs flag malignancy
coreTruths.broaderContext: Most parotid lumps are benign, but the ones that are not behave aggressively. The history and the cranial nerve are the early diagnostic tools, and surgery is first-line for almost everything.
coreTruths.body:
## The parotid story tells the diagnosis

For parotid masses, history and examination are the prime diagnostic tools [1]. A long history without pain and an intact facial nerve points benign. Facial palsy, pain, and rapid growth point malignant. Tumours over 4 cm carry a much higher chance of malignancy [1]. Imaging with CT, USS, or MRI plus FNAC supports the picture, especially when extracapsular dissection rather than conventional superficial parotidectomy is being considered [1].

## Site shifts the prior probability of malignancy hard

The smaller the gland, the more likely a tumour is malignant. Submandibular masses are mostly pleomorphic adenomas, but up to 30 percent are malignant [2]. In sublingual and minor glands, over half of tumours are malignant, mostly adenoid cystic, and a so-called mucocele on the upper lip is almost certainly a tumour [3].

## Surgery comes first for almost every salivary tumour

With the exception of lymphomas, all salivary gland tumours should have surgery first, patient permitting [4]. Parotidectomy aims to remove the tumour with a margin while preserving the facial nerve. Benign superficial-lobe tumours get extracapsular dissection, segmental superficial parotidectomy, or conventional superficial parotidectomy; deep-lobe tumours get total conservative parotidectomy. Malignant tumours need radical excision plus radiotherapy, since radiotherapy alone is almost never curative [5].

## Adenoid cystic carcinoma rewrites the rules of follow-up

Its Swiss-cheese histology and propensity for perineural spread mean it can recur or metastasize to lung years after the primary, and is rarely cured even when long-term survival is possible [6]. Long-term surveillance is the rule.

citations.quote: History and examination are the prime diagnostic tools. Long history, no pain, and no facial nerve involvement suggest benign tumour. Facial palsy, pain, and rapid growth suggest malignancy. Chance of malignancy much greater in tumours >4cm. The feel of many tumours are characteristic. CT, FNAC, USS, &/or MRI may help. This is particularly important if ‘extracapsular dissection’ is the planned treatment rather than conventional segmental parotidectomy.

Less common tumours. Pleomorphic adenoma remains most common. Malignant tumours account for up to 30%. Rx of most is gland excision via a skin crease in the neck. Modified neck dissection (to include level I, II, and III and any locally involved structures such as skin) for malignant or recurrent tumours.

>50% of tumours are malignant (mostly adenoid cystic) and require extensive surgery and reconstruction similar to floor of mouth cancer. Beware the ‘mucocele’ of the upper lip—it is almost certainly a tumour.

Surgery of the major salivary glands is primarily for tumours, obstruction, and, less commonly, inflammatory conditions. The minor glands are most commonly removed for mucoceles (…… Mucoceles, p. 415) and more rarely for tumours. With the exception of lymphomas all salivary gland tumours should have surgery initially, patient permitting.

The principles are complete excision of a tumour with a margin of healthy tissue and preservation of facial nerve. Clinically benign tumours in the superficial lobe have either ‘extracapsular dissection’, segmental superficial parotidectomy, or conventional superficial parotidectomy. In the deep lobe, total conservative parotidectomy. Malignant tumours require radical excision and radiotherapy. Radiotherapy alone is almost never curative.

Adenoid cystic carcinoma—characteristic ‘Swiss cheese’ appearance histologically. Spreads locally, particularly along perineural spaces. Can be compatible with long-term survival despite propensity for secondaries in lungs, although rarely cured.

coreTruths.title: In oral cancer, nodal status and extracapsular spread drive prognosis more than the primary
coreTruths.broaderContext: Oral cancer outcomes hinge on the neck. The size of the primary matters, but what is happening in the lymph nodes — and how aggressively that is treated — is what shifts survival.
coreTruths.body:
## Treatment is staged by TNM, but the patient is staged by their life

Classic principles run on TNM staging plus fitness for surgery, but that framing forgets the patient — their general health, understanding of disease, geography, and social commitments shape the realistic plan as much as the stage [1]. The assumption that a patient too unfit for surgery can travel for and tolerate radiotherapy is not always true [1]. Combined surgery and radiotherapy is often optimal in oral cancer [1].

## The neck decides the prognosis

T1–N0 disease can be treated with surgery or radiotherapy with similar cure rates, and surgery is often simpler with fewer side effects [2]. T2 disease imaged as N0 still carries a 30 percent occult metastasis rate, and most clinicians now favour selective neck dissection over watch-and-wait [3]. T2 and T3 see occult metastases in over half of patients, so the neck gets prophylactic dissection or radiotherapy [4]. Anterior floor-of-mouth cancers can spread bilaterally, so bilateral selective neck dissection is indicated [5].

## Extracapsular spread is the strongest single predictor of poor outcome

The presence of extracapsular spread in cervical lymph nodes is the strongest prognostic indicator of poor outcome [6]. Large tumours, close or positive margins, and extracapsular spread all push the case toward post-operative radiotherapy [7].

## HPV-driven oropharyngeal cancer behaves differently

HPV-16 and -18 drive a growing share of oropharyngeal cancers. In non-smokers, stage for stage these have a much better prognosis with conventional treatment, are probably sexually transmitted, and are entirely preventable by vaccinating pre-sexual children with the same vaccine used for cervical cancer [8].

## Radiotherapy near bone changes the dental plan

If a tumour close to bone is going to have radiotherapy, associated teeth should come out beforehand to prevent osteoradionecrosis [9]. That sits firmly in GDP territory when these patients turn up needing pre-treatment dental clearance.

## Survival is better than the old quoted figures suggest

Figures of 90 percent for T1–N0 falling to 30 percent for T2/3–N1 and worse for T4 are real, but several centres now report better than average 5-year survival with aggressive combined regimens, and HPV-driven cancers do better still [10]. The well-worn line that nothing has improved in 50 years is simply incorrect [10].

citations.quote: Various parameters affect the choice of Rx for patients with oral cancer; not least among these, but often forgotten, are the patients themselves, their general health, understanding of their disease, geographical location, and social and domestic commitments. Classically, broad Rx principles are based on tumour staging, using the Tumour, Node, Metastasis (TNM) classification, and the patient’s fitness for surgery (this tends to imply that if they can’t cope with surgery, they can cope with travelling for and side effects of radiotherapy, which is not always the case). In many instances of oral cancer, combined surgery and radiotherapy constitutes optimal Rx.
T1–N0. Surgery or radiotherapy (including brachytherapy-radioactive implants) offers a similar cure rate. Surgery is often simpler and with less side effects.
T2 but imaging N0. Have a 30% incidence of occult metastases; debate exists over watch and wait or selective neck dissection. Majority favour dissection.

T2 and T3. >50% of patients will have occult metastases; prophylactic radiotherapy (works for occult but not for obvious bulky nodes); or prophylactic selective neck dissection. In presence of imaging or palpable nodes, latter usually best.
Anterior floor of mouth cancer may spread to bilateral lymph nodes; bilateral selective neck dissection is indicated.
Presence or absence of extracapsular spread in cervical lymph nodes is strongest prognostic indicator of poor outcome.
For large tumours, close or +ve margins, and extracapsular spread, radiotherapy given post-operatively.

HPV-16 and -18 have become important causes of oropharyngeal cancer. In non-smokers, stage for stage these cancers have a very much better prognosis when treated with conventional techniques. It is probably sexually transmitted (although the exact nature and why most people clear oral HPV infection within a year are not fully understood). It is entirely preventable by vaccination of pre-sexual children with the same vaccine girls are receiving to prevent cervical cancer in most developed countries.
Tumour close to bone having radiotherapy: safest to remove associated teeth to prevent osteoradionecrosis.

Several centres are reporting better-than-average 5yr survival figures with aggressive combination treatment regimens and identification of HPV-driven cancers means much of the previously widely held beliefs with regard to survival (often quoted as there has been no improvement in the last 50 years) should be reconsidered as they are simply incorrect.
